questions.text: Which one of the following regular expressions correctly represents the language of the finite automaton given below?
questions.solution:
The start state is not final. From start:
- on a go to the upper final state (loops on b, returns to start on b) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] one round trip is [latex]ab^*b[/latex];
- on b go to the lower final state (loops on a, returns to start on a) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] one round trip is [latex]ba^*a[/latex].

So: any number of round trips [latex](ab^*b+ba^*a)^*[/latex], and then finish in one of the final states: [latex]ab^*[/latex] or [latex]ba^*[/latex].

Answer: [latex](ba^*a+ab^*b)^*(ab^*+ba^*)[/latex]

questions.text: Which of the following regular expressions represent(s) the set of all binary numbers that are divisible by three? Assume that the string [latex]\epsilon[/latex] is divisible by three.
questions.solution:
The DFA for "value mod 3" has states 0, 1, 2 (start and final 0); reading bit b moves r to [latex](2r+b)\bmod3[/latex].
- Option 1: from state 0, "0" stays; "1" goes to 1, [latex](01^*0)^*[/latex] loops 1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 1, and the final "1" returns to 0 True
- Option 2: same paths written differently (11, or 10 to state 2, loop, 01 back) True
- Option 3: [latex](0^*X^*)^*=(0+X)^*[/latex] where X is the loop in option 1 True
- Option 4: cannot produce 1001 (= 9, divisible by 3) False

Answer: Options 1, 2 and 3

questions.text:
For a string [latex]w[/latex], we define [latex]w^R[/latex] to be the reverse of [latex]w[/latex]. For example, if [latex]w=01101[/latex] then [latex]w^R=10110[/latex].
Which of the following languages is/are context-free?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- [latex]wxw^Rx^R[/latex]: the w-pair and x-pair cross each other [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] not CFL.
- [latex]ww^Rxx^R[/latex]: two even palindromes one after another [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] CFL.
- [latex]wxw^R[/latex]: take w = [latex]\epsilon[/latex], so it is all of [latex]\{0,1\}^*[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] regular, hence CFL.
- [latex]wxx^Rw^R[/latex]: nested matching (an even palindrome) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] CFL.

Answer: Options 2, 3 and 4

questions.text:
Consider the following two statements about regular languages:

S1: Every infinite regular language contains an undecidable language as a subset.
S2: Every finite language is regular.

Which one of the following choices is correct?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- S1: an infinite language has uncountably many subsets, but only countably many are decidable. So some subset is undecidable [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- S2: a finite language is a finite union of single strings [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] regular [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Both S1 and S2 are true

options: Both S1 and S2 are true
Neither S1 nor S2 is true

questions.text:
Suppose we want to design a synchronous circuit that processes a string of 0's and 1's. Given a string, it produces another string by replacing the first 1 in any subsequence of consecutive 1's by a 0. Consider the following example.

[latex]\begin{array}{ll} \text{Input sequence:} & 00100011000011100 \\ \text{Output sequence:} & 00000001000001100 \end{array}[/latex]

A Mealy Machine is a state machine where both the next state and the output are functions of the present state and the current input.
The above mentioned circuit can be designed as a two-state Mealy machine. The states in the Mealy machine can be represented using Boolean values 0 and 1. We denote the current state, the next state, the next incoming bit, and the output bit of the Mealy machine by the variables s, t, b and y respectively.
Assume the initial state of the Mealy machine is 0.

What are the Boolean expressions corresponding to t and y in terms of s and b?
questions.solution:
The state remembers the previous bit: t = b.

Output 1 only for a 1 that is not the first of a run, i.e. the current bit is 1 and the previous bit was 1: y = sb.

Check with 0011: outputs 0, 0, 0, 1 True

Answer: t = b, y = sb
